rationale: UEM/MDM is explicitly described as 'the enforcement backbone for all other capabilities' — it operationalizes the seven-capability framework.
Real-time deny-by-default enrollment requires centralized management to enforce enrollment decisions and maintain the authoritative device registry.
Risk-based authorization cannot function without knowing what devices exist — inventory is the foundational input.
Compliance status and policy enforcement data are essential inputs to the risk calculation engine for authorization decisions.
Event-Condition-Action automation provides the continuous posture-checking mechanism that feeds real-time risk signals into authorization.
Hardware-bound identity (TPM/HSM) provides stronger, tamper-resistant signals for risk calculations than software-only credentials.
Trust degradation over time is a specific risk factor that continuous authorization must account for — device age is framed as the strongest negative signal.
Cross-pillar dependencies mean device authorization inherently requires identity and network inputs, reinforcing the need for multi-signal risk assessment.
The EDR→XDR progression is the specific technical mechanism that enables centralized, unified threat protection across all devices.
Evidence states threat protection is 'integrated with policy enforcement and compliance monitoring' — centralized threat data feeds compliance visibility.
BeyondCorp at Google was the large-scale proof that the seven-capability model (inventory, certificates, SSO, access proxy) works in production.
BeyondCorp used TPM-stored corporate-issued certificates as the root of trust — a direct implementation of hardware-bound device identity.
Distributed enforcement across four layers (intra-VLAN through host-level) is a concrete implementation of device-aware resource access decisions.
Resource access decisions that consider real-time device risk analytics require a continuous risk-based authorization engine.
Heightened scrutiny for hostile remote environments is a specific intensification of continuous risk-based authorization — same flow, stricter thresholds.
Both expand vulnerability management beyond traditional CVE scanning: firmware goes deeper below the OS layer, behavioral baselines go broader across communication patterns.
Supply chain risk management extends device inventory to include vendor/service provider assets and their associated risks — inventory is the foundation, supply chain adds the vendor dimension.
Contract provisions and third-party risk management are the primary operational mechanism for implementing supply chain risk controls.
The systemic vulnerability created by integrator gaps is the specific threat that supply chain risk management must address — it provides the problem statement.
Visibility & Analytics and Automation & Orchestration (the cross-cutting capabilities) are the enablers that make ECA automation technically feasible.
Unpatched firmware below the OS is a key vector by which device trust degrades over time — firmware neglect accelerates trust decay.
Policy enforcement and compliance monitoring require centralized management (UEM/MDM) to push policies, collect compliance data, and remediate across the fleet.
IoT's closed systems, weak authentication, and unpatchable firmware fundamentally prevent the universal centralized management that UEM/MDM assumes.
Unpatchable IoT firmware directly contradicts the requirement that patch management must cover firmware below the OS — these devices are unmanageable by design.
